profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a mid-sized bank to evaluate a draft methodology note and slide deck for updating the operational risk severity-model validation standard. The proposal recommends keeping maximum likelihood estimation for fitting heavy-tailed loss severities, while adding a short section on when asymptotic normality can be relied on for parameter confidence intervals. The context is that Model Risk Committee wants a 'design-ready' review before the note is circulated to validation and internal audit. The agenda is to assess whether the proposed review package is complete enough for committee circulation, whether the examples and caveats are sufficient for business users, and what modifications are needed. The expected outcome is agreement on revisions and a decision to move the package forward for committee pre-read.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: Operational risk capital frameworks, severity modeling, model governance documentation
members.background: Priya spent eight years in enterprise risk modeling and now owns methodology standards for non-financial risk models across the bank.
members.private_state: She wants the package to clear committee with minimal rework, avoid opening a broader debate about replacing MLE, and keep the standard practical for business-line model owners with thin data.
hidden_assumptions: 'Design-ready' means the methodology note is conceptually complete for committee review even if appendices, worked examples, and implementation wording are refined afterward.
When the package says 'small sample,' readers will naturally interpret it as the typical bank-level severity samples of roughly 30-80 losses above threshold per unit of measure.
The 'confidence interval section' is about parameter intervals around fitted severity parameters, since that is what validation usually challenges directly.
The proposed 'simulation check' can be done as a lightweight sensitivity illustration in the methodology appendix rather than a full rerun for every production unit.
References to the 'current lognormal example' obviously point to the benchmark example in the methodology note, not the separate committee appendix.

members.name: Daniel Wu
members.expertise: Statistical validation, tail-model diagnostics, review standards for risk quantification models
members.background: Daniel previously worked in quantitative audit and now leads independent validation reviews for operational risk and stress testing models.
members.private_state: He wants the document to be defensible under validation challenge, make limitations of asymptotic normality explicit enough to survive audit, and avoid any wording that sounds like blanket approval of normal-based intervals in sparse data settings.
hidden_assumptions: 'Design-ready' means committee circulation should include near-final evidence, examples, and reviewer-reproducible detail so that no substantive methodological gaps remain.
When people say 'small sample' in this context, they mean the truly sparse cells that drive validation concern, often fewer than 25 threshold exceedances.

The 'confidence interval section' should address the practical output used in governance decisions, namely intervals or uncertainty statements around capital or high-quantile loss estimates, not just parameter estimates.
A 'simulation check' implies a documented validation-style exercise with repeated sampling under the proposed fitted distributions and explicit coverage results.
References to the 'current lognormal example' naturally mean the committee appendix example that already includes the 99.9th percentile impact table.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the package should be 'design-ready' for Model Risk Committee.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means the core argument, governance framing, and recommended caveats are complete enough for committee discussion, even if supporting examples and appendix wording are polished afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means the package should already contain the supporting examples, evidence, and near-final methodological detail needed for reviewers to test whether the proposal is acceptable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In governance settings, 'design-ready' sounds like a standard maturity label, so both hear it as shared project language and do not naturally restate the threshold for completeness.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether asymptotic normality is reliable in 'small samples.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya is thinking of moderately limited operational risk datasets, roughly 30-80 losses above threshold, where she wants nuanced caution but not a broad warning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel is thinking of the sparsest cells, often under 25 losses, where asymptotic approximations are most visibly unreliable and where validation objections usually arise.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'small sample' is ubiquitous in model review and usually treated as self-explanatory; each person maps it to the cases most salient in their work without noticing the numeric mismatch.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the note needs a stronger section on 'confidence intervals around the MLE results.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means intervals for fitted distribution parameters such as shape and scale, because that is the methodological focus of the note and the cited paper.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means uncertainty statements for downstream outputs that matter in governance, especially tail quantiles and capital figures derived from the fitted parameters.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because downstream outputs come from the same fitted model, talking about 'MLE results' feels naturally inclusive; neither sees a need to distinguish parameter-level from business-output uncertainty in a short review conversation.

misalignment_points.topic: Which lognormal example is being referenced
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the current lognormal example' as evidence for how much extra explanation is needed.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya is referring to the benchmark example in the main methodology note, which compares Wald intervals with profile-likelihood intervals on a 60-loss sample.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel is referring to the committee appendix example, which shows how parameter uncertainty changes the 99.9th percentile estimate for a business unit.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There are two active draft artifacts circulated in the same workstream, each with a prominent lognormal example, so the phrase sounds specific enough while actually pointing to different documents.

turns.inner_thought: I want to keep this tightly scoped: retain MLE, add sensible caveats, and get something conceptually complete in front of committee without inviting a rewrite of the whole standard. For me, design-ready means the main note and governance framing are settled; we can still refine appendices and examples after the review.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. The main objective today is to confirm whether the package is design-ready for Model Risk Committee circulation. The core recommendation hasn't changed: we retain MLE for severity fitting, but we sharpen the caveats around when asymptotic normality should and shouldn't be leaned on.

turns.inner_thought: The direction is fine, but I don't want this going to committee with only high-level statements. Design-ready, to me, means reviewers can actually see the evidence, examples, and enough detail to test the claims. Otherwise validation and audit will push it straight back.
turns.utterance: That direction makes sense to me. For something to be design-ready, though, I'd want confidence that the caveats are supported by enough visible evidence, not just principle-level wording. If reviewers are going to challenge it, the package should already show why the guardrails are there.

turns.inner_thought: I need the language to be cautious without sounding like asymptotic normality is unusable. In the kinds of severity samples I usually see, it's often serviceable with warnings. I should keep it at the level of larger samples versus small samples and not put numbers on the table.
turns.utterance: Right. The proposed wording basically says that asymptotic normality is often acceptable in larger samples, but becomes less dependable in small samples, especially once you're dealing with heavier-tailed severities.

turns.inner_thought: I agree with that framing, but my concern is the truly sparse cells where the approximation can be badly misleading. I don't want any reader to come away thinking normal-based intervals are broadly fine in small samples. I'll stress material understatement of uncertainty, but keep the wording general.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think in small samples we should be a little more explicit that normal-based approximations can materially understate uncertainty in the cases validation is most worried about. The note doesn't need to overstate it, but it should be hard to misread.

turns.inner_thought: Validation usually comes after the fitted severity parameters, and that's where the cited literature is strongest. I can strengthen that section without opening a broader debate about output-level uncertainty and capital methodology. A short caution on Wald intervals should be enough.
turns.utterance: Understood. One thing I can do is strengthen the section on confidence intervals around the MLE results. I think a short additional paragraph on when Wald-style intervals should be treated cautiously would make the note more balanced.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but committee won't care only about interval mechanics in the abstract. They'll want to see what this means for reported risk numbers, especially in the tail. I'll phrase it as linking the confidence interval discussion to practical outputs, without spelling out the exact downstream metrics.
turns.utterance: I support that. I do think the committee will want the confidence interval discussion tied to what happens to reported risk numbers when asymptotic normality is weak. Otherwise the point may feel too technical relative to the governance decision.

turns.inner_thought: The benchmark lognormal example in the methodology note already shows the comparison I need; it just needs a cleaner caption and a sentence about how behavior changes as sample size gets smaller. I don't want to build out a whole new worked case if I can avoid it.
turns.utterance: That's fair. My view is that the current lognormal example already gets most of the message across; it may just need a clearer caption and one sentence on sample-size sensitivity so the reader sees why the caveat is there.

turns.inner_thought: The committee appendix example is useful, but right now it doesn't make the uncertainty effect explicit enough for a reviewer trying to assess impact on the tail estimate. I'd like it to show the consequence more directly, but I'll just refer to the current lognormal example so this still sounds aligned.
turns.utterance: I agree the current lognormal example is helpful. I think it would land better if it showed the uncertainty effect a bit more directly, so the committee can immediately see why the caution matters rather than infer it from the surrounding text.

turns.inner_thought: A lightweight appendix simulation should satisfy this without turning into a validation program. I mean a simple sensitivity illustration, probably around the benchmark fit, just enough to show interval behavior degrades in small samples. I definitely don't want to imply a full production rerun across units.
turns.utterance: Another option is to add a brief simulation check in the appendix. That would let us show that the asymptotic interval behaves less well in small samples, without turning the note into a research paper.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, a simulation check would help, but I mean something documented enough that a reviewer can see repeated-sampling behavior and judge coverage in the sparse cases that create real validation concern. If that's in the package, I can probably support design-ready status.
turns.utterance: Yes, a simulation check would definitely help. It should be enough for reviewers to see whether the interval behavior is acceptable in the edge cases that matter most. If that evidence is there, it goes a long way toward making the package feel design-ready.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll update the methodology note, tighten the caveats, refresh the benchmark example, and add an appendix simulation illustration. That should be sufficient for committee discussion while leaving room to polish wording later. As long as Daniel feels broadly comfortable, we can keep this moving.
turns.utterance: Okay, that's workable. I'll revise the draft so it's design-ready with expanded caveats, the updated lognormal example, and a tighter confidence interval section. I'll also add the appendix check so the rationale is more visible.

turns.inner_thought: Assuming the updated materials actually show the evidence I expect, I should be able to support committee pre-read. I still need near-final detail in the examples and uncertainty discussion, but her summary sounds aligned enough that I don't need to reopen the bigger MLE question right now.
turns.utterance: That sounds good from my side. With those revisions, I should be comfortable for committee pre-read, and I think the package will land well if the evidence is visible in the updated materials.
